summary: Re-review of the ten changed blocks plus all programmatic flags. The v1 must_fix (L1, 'schutting' → 'hek') and all eight should_fix items (L2–L9) are fixed; L7 was applied in a variant (knife kept as its own sentence to avoid a vocab cluster) that still breaks the 'Toen' chain and adds the 'op' particle. The grammar table is clean: R-DAT on the bible chunk is now whitelisted; the three remaining review-level flags are a polite 'Zou u', a modal + copular 'klinken' mis-read as a passive because 'verdacht' is participle-shaped, and a zijn-perfectum of 'komen'. The new wording uses only A1/A2 words (kachel, heet, snel, verschijnen, hek, oppas, nou), no new unknown lemmas, 13 glosses matching the text, stretch budget still 7 of 8. No new must_fix or should_fix; seven notes, mostly carried vocabulary and policy observations for the lexicon owner.

findings.fragment: Een platte plaat van metaal op een deur
findings.problem: Carried from v1 L11: 'plaat van metaal' is a workaround for the lexicon rating the material adjective 'metalen' B2 while 'metaal' is A2; the natural phrase is 'een platte metalen plaat'.
findings.evidence: lexicon metaal known A2, metalen hard B2; @notes b055
findings.required_fix: Optional: 'Een platte metalen plaat op een deur nodigt uit tot duwen.' once the lexicon derives -en material adjectives from the known noun (tool_feedback).

findings.fragment: \emph{Brief voor Zweinstein!} roepen, met een envelop hoog in de lucht, midden in je eigen achtertuin. Dat was…
findings.problem: Carried from v1 L12: verbless infinitive phrase standing as its own sentence, resumed by 'Dat' (left dislocation). All words known and the finite clause follows at once, so it stays; noted so that s04's bare exclamative infinitive is judged the same way.
findings.evidence: not flagged by the checker; restricted.md R-PARTICIPLE covers clause-replacing reductions, which this is not

findings.problem: The three unglossed 'unknown' rows with action 'review' are not vocabulary problems: 'grafiet' is a transparent cognate (graphite), 'zakmes' a compound of two A1 words (zak + mes), 'H.J.P.E.V.' Harry's initials.
findings.evidence: vocab rows grafiet / zakmes / h.j.p.e.v.: unknown, action review; lexicon zak, mes known A1; initials fixed by the bible
findings.required_fix: No change. Lexicon owner: add 'grafiet' to cognates, let compound splitting resolve 'zakmes', treat dotted initials as names.

findings.problem: The seven glossed unknowns are justified: everyday words missing from the lexicon (gootsteen, gênant, vulpotlood), a derivation of a known verb (toelating ← toelaten A2), the bible's term for 'falsify' (weerleggen) and two words the translator keeps glossed rather than raise the unglossed-unknown count (kalligrafie, a cognate; haarnetje, haar + net + -je). No paragraph exceeds two glosses; the 13 @glosses lines match the 13 \gl in the text.

flag_decisions.span: Dat moest eigenlijk heel verdacht klinken
flag_decisions.reason: No 'worden' or 'zijn' in the sentence: modal 'moest' + bare copular infinitive 'klinken' (A-MODAL) with the predicate adjective 'verdacht' (lexicon ADJ, A2). The parser took 'verdacht' for the participle of 'verdenken'. New flag produced by the v1 L6 split; false positive.

flag_decisions.span: de brief is hier op een of andere manier gekomen
flag_decisions.reason: Perfectum of the intransitive 'komen' with 'zijn' (look-alike 'Hij is gevallen'); no agent, no passive reading possible.

'verbaasd' is a lexicon adjective (A1) used attributively directly before its noun ('een verbaasde vrouwenstem'); restricted.md: simple adjectival participles in the lexicon are fine. Reported at ignore level.

tool_feedback.ref: R-PASSIVE review 0.30 'Dat moest eigenlijk heel verdacht klinken'
tool_feedback.reason: The checker's own note says 'no worden/zijn: copular?'. When the sentence has no form of worden/zijn and the suspected participle is a lexicon ADJ (verdacht, bekend, gesloten, verbaasd …) after a copular verb (zijn, lijken, klinken, worden-as-become, blijven, voelen), do not report; at most ignore level.
